messages.author: 3b679b7acf28007c
messages.subject: Censored Data - User Manual Page 107 !
parts:
Hi,

I wanted to ask for some clarification on how stan works with survival (censored) data. Before asking my question, I think it would be helpful that I start with the likelihood in survival analysis:

Likelihood contribution of subject i = L_i = f(t_i)^{d_i} S(t_i)^{1 - di}   

where :

t_i = either the event time or the time the subject got censored

d_i = observing indicator (if the event observed is 1, and 0 if we didn't get to see the event (censored))

f(t_i) = probability density of death at t_i

S(t_i) = 1 - CDF(t_i)

The likelihood above means that:

1) if subject i dies at t_i ----> we increment the log likelihood by log(f(t_i))

2) if subject i gets censored at t_i (he dies later but we don't get to see it) ----> we increment the log likelihood by log(S(t_i))


The logic above is what exactly explained on page 108 and 109 of the user manual. In specific, the code on the top of page 109, explains that :

y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma) ---> i.e. incrementing log likelihood by log of density at observed times 

increment_log_prob(N_cens*normal_cdf_log(U, mu, sigma)); -----> incrementing log likelihood by log survival for censored subjects.


Here is the question: on page 107, there is a piece of code where its model block reads as:

y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma) ------> as before, this is equivalent to increment log likelihood by log density at observed times

y_cens ~ normal(mu, sigma) -----> Is this equivalent to incrementing log likelihood by log(s(t)) ?


Why I'm asking this?

We know S(t) = 1 - CDF = 1 - \int f(z) dz. Suppose evaluating S(t) requires the actual integration, then incrementing log likelihood by log (s(t)) for censored observations is difficult as it requires integration. However, the trick on page 107 where censored data are treated as parameters with a lower bound of their censoring times, can help us avoid dealing with S(t). Maybe by defining censored times as parameters, STAN by itself deals with S(t) under the hood without users interference? 

If instead of computing S(t), I could use this trick, then dealing with cases with more complicated S(t) would become very handy. One such example is when we have covariates that are functions of time in our survival analysis.


Thanks very much for your help,

It's technically a different density with different
numbers of parameters, so the posterior's technically different.

But, if you ignore y_cens (effectively marginalize it out),
you get the same inferences for the remaining parameters.

It's usually better to do the explicit marginalization
when possible, but that can require some hairy numerics
in the CDFs, so the results will probably vary by distribution.

Suppose evaluating S(t) requires the actual integration, then incrementing log likelihood by log (s(t)) for censored observations is difficult as it requires integration. Right. That's why this technique's generally useful. It also
lets you continue to think generatively and impute missing values
in one go.
